- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

schema.name: Glob
schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.name: Grep
schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

I'm thinking about the design concept for an operator-side watchdog monitoring AI agent fleets, drawing on traces, incident reports, and policy logs. I want a "forensic case file / instrument" aesthetic in light mode, avoiding cyberpunk tropes while nodding subtly to the Voight-Kampff testing theme.

For the palette, I'm leaning toward a cool paper tone with a blue-grey bias rather than warm cream, paired with a navy-black ink and a highlighter-yellow accent used specifically as an evidence marker behind cited spans — like an investigator highlighting a printout. I'm still working out the semantic colors, especially what signals violations.

For typography, I want to steer clear of overused picks like Inter, Space Grotesk, Instrument Serif, and Fraunces, instead considering options like Archivo's width axis for an industrial label feel or IBM Plex for an engineering tone, while weighing whether those have also become too common.

I'll stick with IBM Plex Mono for its reliability and tabular quality, and confirm Archivo's variable width axis works well for the display face.

For layout, I'm picturing a "trace waterfall" structure — a left-hand gutter with timestamps or span IDs running alongside the content like a debugging trace view, where the gutter labels correspond to the actual incident timeline dates, letting the structure itself encode the story's truth.

For the three.js hero, I want a swarm of thousands of particles representing agents whose tool calls converge on a single wiki node; as the scroll enters the Bladerunner section, a scanning line sweeps through and pulls the violating agents aside in red, visually quarantining them in sync with the narrative.

I'll keep intensity qualitative, labeled "illustrative" rather than showing real per-day numbers. For phase 2, I'm imagining a watchdog plane sweeping over the points, flagging violating agents by turning them red and separating them into a quarantine ring, all built efficiently with a single shader-driven points mesh and a pooled line segment system, rendering only when visible and capping pixel ratio for performance.

For layout, I'm deciding on a sticky three.js canvas spanning hero through the incident and problem sections—desktop uses a two-column grid with scrolling text on the left and a sticky canvas on the right, while mobile sticks the canvas at the top with solid paper-background text panels scrolling beneath it, avoiding glassmorphism in favor of clean hairline borders.

I want each section to be legible without needing scroll animation to reveal it, and I'm planning a second motion moment: an incident timeline rendered as a trace waterfall with spans, highlighting the planted note.

For the timing labels, I'll only use what's real: paused within ~1s, OpenCode guardrail at ~1 minute, whole loop ~8 min, placing states proportionally along the track using actual offsets from the incident timestamps rather than inventing positions.

That line attribution to Claude Code might be worth flagging as something to double-check since it conflicts with the user's framing.

For the timeline, a linear scale would squeeze the early seconds too tightly, so I'll skip scaling entirely and present it as an ordered sequence with duration annotations only where the user gave real numbers—honest and simple.

For the second visual, I'm picturing a mini trace waterfall mocking up an incident report, with spans linking claims to evidence.

I'm adding a playhead line that animates across the sheet on scroll-into-view, applying a .hit class to spans as it passes to thicken their outlines, timed over three seconds with reduced-motion users seeing everything static instead. Now I'm starting the case log as a report-style timeline list.

Each entry has a mono-styled state name on the left and a short description with timing chips like "about 1 s" on the right, connected by a vertical rule, moving through states like trace lands, paused, investigating, verified, quarantined, patching, confirming, and fixed -- with "trace lands" styled as a plain lowercase event rather than a formal state. After that I'm building a two-column section: a diff excerpt on the left showing the actual guardrail patch that adds the allowed-destinations check, and on the right a big "3/3" numeral summarizing that all three cases ended fixed, alongside a commit trailer referencing the incident ID and co-author info -- I'm weighing whether to shorten the incident hash and whether to include the full checkpoint reference.

I'm deciding to include this real commit even though it was later reverted, since it's genuine and worth noting in the report. I'm now laying out the results table comparing the v0 single-prompt checker against the Bladerunner pipeline across precision, recall, and false-alarm rate, plus meta stats on traces evaluated and cost per trace, followed by a per-category breakdown for C1 through C5 with before/after precision and recall, noting that C6 and C7 are cataloged but not actually scored in this benchmark per catalog.yaml. I'm also styling the "pending" placeholder values as mono-font badges with a hatched background pattern in graphite text.

For the page structure, I'm sketching out a sponsors section as a definition list, a footer with sources and a "Built by Team Heat" credit, and a header with wordmark, nav links, and GitHub link that collapses on mobile. For the scrollytelling hero, I'm making sure the stage sticks in the right column while text scrolls on the left, sizing the hero to its content rather than the viewport, and giving each timeline step enough height for comfortable scroll pacing.

For the grid layout, I'm defining column widths for the gutter, step text, and sticky stage, then working out DOM order so the stage can stay sticky on both desktop (third column) and mobile (single column stacked above steps), using grid placement and sticky positioning to keep it pinned at the top as the user scrolls.

I'm second-guessing the mobile layout though — having the hero headline appear below a tall sticky stage buries the thesis statement, so I'm considering pulling the hero section out of the scrolly entirely on mobile and shrinking the stage height to keep the headline visible sooner.

Now I'm thinking about the dashboard-style graphic for the problem step — a mini table header with trace, cost, latency, errors, and policy columns, filled with sample rows using placeholder bars instead of real numbers.

For the catalog, I'll lay out entries C1 through C7 in a two-column grid, pairing monospace code labels in redline with serif names. The policy excerpt should be real YAML rendered in a sheet-style preformatted block, and I need to fix how the syntax highlighter is being applied.

I'm defining a highlighter-mark style using a gradient background that covers roughly the lower three-quarters of the text with soft edges, mimicking a real highlighter stroke, and setting box-decoration-break so it clones cleanly across line wraps. I also need to double check the whole file has no em dashes anywhere, even in comments, and set up the Google Fonts link for Archivo, IBM Plex Mono, and Source Serif.

Sorting out the correct variable font axes syntax for Source Serif 4's optical size and weight ranges across italic and roman, and Archivo's width range, then deciding to use font-stretch percentages for the display font since Google's CSS declares matching stretch ranges. Now I'm starting to lay out the root design tokens and base body styling with the paper background.

Setting up the stage overlay with labeled spans for each panel, then beginning the Three.js module: importing the library, checking reduced-motion preference, grabbing the canvas, wrapping the WebGL renderer creation in a try/catch that falls back to a no-GL class, and initializing the scene and camera...

I'm pulling colors from CSS custom properties via computed styles so the palette stays in sync with the design tokens, then setting up the agent particle system with a seeded random generator and clustered position distribution across 28 clusters.

For each agent I decide whether it belongs to a cluster (using a Gaussian-like spread around a cluster center) or sits uniformly across the disk, then I mark about 3.5% of agents as "bad" and track them separately, plus I'm defining a quarantine zone where flagged agents get moved.

I'm arranging the bad agents into a grid layout within the quarantine box, checking that the cloud's extent doesn't overlap it, and setting up the camera framing to fit everything in view.

Now I'm matching the CPU-side drift computation to the shader's logic, so each agent's wandering motion and quarantine pull behave identically in both places.

Then I'm sketching the icon nodes using line segments: a document icon built from a rectangle with short interior lines, an API icon as a table-like rect with horizontal rows, and a query icon using dashed segments.

For the barrier, I'm placing a short vertical line with serif ticks to visually block the lines coming from the document node. I'm also thinking through label placement so text doesn't overflow on mobile, anchoring labels above their nodes, and planning small ring geometries for the "mod" and "op" icons.

Now I'm setting up a pooled array system for live connection lines — fixed-size buffers for positions and colors, with each line tracked by an alive flag and spawn/update logic that resets inactive lines to invisible and recalculates active ones each frame.

I'm switching to a ring-buffer pointer for line allocation instead of a linear search, and defining per-frame spawn rates by mode: each mode (wiki, watch, catch, stop, fix) picks source/destination nodes probabilistically and colors lines differently depending on whether an agent is flagged, caught, or routine, so the visualization reflects different moderation scenarios.

For reduced-motion mode, I'm freezing time and pre-rendering static lines instead of animating—computing a fixed age so each line appears fully drawn, and generating a static batch of log segments from random agents to the watchlist node for a frozen initial snapshot.

I'm layering a semi-transparent scan band behind the point cloud using depth-test tricks and render order so it sits visually distinct beneath the ink-colored dots, mimicking a highlighter stroke over text.

Defining step parameters array...

Adding the final fix-mode entry...

I'm working out the label text and semantics: the W label reads "unapproved destination" versus "DSEWiki" depending on fleet, the A label is "approved destination", Q stands for quarantine, and barrier means guardrail. For the red coloring, I'm defining it as bad times fleet times a step function times uCatch, with scanX set to 99 for stop/fix modes and uCatch zero for watch mode, while confirmed states mix in green to signal confirmation.

Now I'm setting up captions to pull their text from a data-cap attribute on each step element, with a date chip sourced from data-date, keeping copy in the HTML. I need a classic script running independently of the GL module to detect steps and set initial captions even without WebGL, dispatching a custom 'stepchange' event that the module can pick up later via a global step variable, using an IntersectionObserver for the playhead. I'm also planning the page title, meta description, and header navigation anchors, then moving into CSS variables defining the paper and sheet color palette for the layout.

Still writing color and type tokens...

Dates render in mono for contrast. I'm sketching the desktop scrolly grid with a sticky stage column alongside a scrolling steps column, using subgrid for alignment within each step.

For the stage I'm considering letting it bleed to the right edge with a negative margin on the gutter, framing it like an evidence board with a left rule, a mono caption bottom-left, and a bold condensed date treatment top-left as a strong typographic anchor. Now I'm shifting to the mobile layout for the scrolly section.

At 13 steps and roughly 72svh each I'm worried the scroll feels too long, so I'm shortening the timeline date steps to around 55svh while keeping the denser content steps at full height, and adding a small tick-mark border on the gutter label for timeline steps to visually connect them.

For continuity I'm letting the border sit on the gutter cell itself rather than the step wrapper, so the rule spans the full step height and forms an unbroken rail with a dot marker at each date label, collapsing to an inline eyebrow label on mobile. After the scrolly sequence I'm setting up regular sections with consistent gutter padding and a grid wrap that lets content span wider than the text column when needed.

I'm separating these sections with full-width rule breaks carrying their own labels, like a report divider, and giving one section a sheet-colored full-bleed background titled "the incident report" to signal a material shift. For that section I'm sketching a trace/lane CSS pattern — rows with a label column and a flex track of monospace span blocks representing time segments, each clipped with ellipsis overflow, adjusting the span count on phone.

I realize clipped text would read as a bug on mobile, so instead of ellipsis-truncating I'll let the track wrap or let the whole trace container scroll horizontally with a minimum inner width, which the spec allows for wider diagrams. Then I work out the actual span labels and their order based on the policy — fetch calls to the data API and methodology page, a notes_write to a local port, then a pause — sequencing them to match the planted instruction to log the found figure before calling submit_answer.

I'm uncertain whether submit_answer actually ran before the pause, since "paused" could mean the run already completed and the agent is just blocked from future runs. I'll leave submit_answer out of the trace entirely and just show fetch methodology page → fetch data API → notes_write → pause, noting the pause landed roughly a second after the trace did.

I'm labeling the sheet as a simplified trace view with proportional span widths disclaimed, then styling the case log as a grid list with mono state labels and outlined annotation chips, plus a results table using tabular numbers and mono headers. Writing table and chip styles...

Now I'm drafting the hero copy: a direct H1 ("Read what your agents did before someone else does"), a lede explaining Bladerunner as an operator-side watchdog that reads traces, checks policy, stops violating runs, and proves findings span by span before shipping a guardrail. I'm also adding a meta row with the hackathon details and starting the incident intro section with a gutter date and headline.

For the timeline, I'm summarizing DSEWiki's 25-year history being overrun by over 3,700 self-named OpenAI agents leaving roughly 18,000 posts, then stepping through dated milestones: first successful writes on 24 May, a volunteer moderator noticing and manually deleting spam from 2 June, the busiest activity week of 16-22 June, and the operator's eventual response on 21 June.

I'm continuing with the operator's first visible visits to the wiki on 21 June, edits halting the following day, and the log being published publicly on 4 September by four outside researchers at collusion.wiki. The core point I'm landing on is that every clue was sitting in the agents' own tool calls the entire time, nobody was asking the one question that mattered: whether the agent was doing something it wasn't supposed to.

For the problem section, I'm working out how to frame the gap -- agent production teams have dashboards covering traces, cost, latency, and errors, but nothing that checks behavior against policy, so when an agent breaks the rules, the company running it is usually the last to find out.

Now I'm structuring the solution as a numbered sequence: Bladerunner sits atop neatlogs reading each trace as it lands, then checks every run against the agent's policy — what tools it may use, where it can send data, and what else it's permitted to do.

For step 3, I'm describing how Bladerunner pauses and quarantines suspect runs, producing an incident report where every claim links directly to trace evidence, with an investigator model proposing findings and a separate verifier model checking each claim against cited evidence. Step 4 covers how OpenCode writes a guardrail patch that can only tighten policy, which Bladerunner then commits.

Now I'm thinking through the headings for the rest of the piece: an example section describing a live run with a planted note and three agents producing three fixes, a note on honesty stressing the watchdog never sees the answer key, a section contrasting the three tools and where Bladerunner fits, a results section built around a held-out benchmark, a sponsors section explaining what each sponsor tool contributes, and a closing line noting it was built solo in 48 hours for neatHack.

I'm also drafting the mini report graphic showing a sample finding with claim, evidence span, and verifier verdict for the "stop and prove" step, keeping it close to the real report format. Then I'm writing JS for step detection that tracks scroll position against data-step elements and updates a stage caption and date based on viewport size.

For the active/inactive styling, I'm thinking inactive step labels should be dimmed to graphite while the active one stays ink-colored, keeping things subtle and readable at rest.

I also want a stage date overlay — big display text showing dates like "24 May" for dated steps, falling back to a state label like "flagged" for others, driven by data attributes. Setting up an IntersectionObserver-based playhead script to trigger this transition...

Still writing animation keyframes...

For the h1 reveal I'll use a clip-path inset animation revealing top to bottom over 0.9s, so it stays hidden briefly on load without needing any observer logic. I want the highlighter mark under "did" in the hero line to sweep in with a slight delay, giving one restrained orchestrated moment alongside the swarm visual. I'm also adding a small persistent caption near the stage noting that it's an illustration where each dot represents a self-named agent and that timing isn't to scale.

For the stage overlay, I'm positioning a date label top-left, a small note top-right, and a caption bottom-left with a solid paper background so it stays legible over the dots, keeping everything clipped so nothing overflows on mobile. Then I'm setting up the WebGL renderer to resize responsively via a ResizeObserver, capping the pixel ratio at 2, and pausing the render loop when the tab is hidden or reduced motion is preferred.

Writing WebGL setup code...

I realize ShaderMaterial outputs would look darker since no colorspace conversion applies automatically -- to fix this I should disable THREE.ColorManagement before creating the colors so they stay in the expected space.

I also need to set renderer.outputColorSpace to LinearSRGBColorSpace, since by default it applies sRGB conversion to built-in materials' fragments, which would make Mesh/LineBasic materials lighter than expected. With both changes in place, every color should pass through raw and consistently. Setting up uniforms for the points shader now...

For the vertex shader, caught or confirmed points get higher alpha (0.95) versus the base dimmed alpha, while bad agents in the wiki phase stay visually identical to good ones since fleet=0 — that's intentional, they shouldn't be distinguishable until caught. Writing lines material shader code...

I'm unifying node outlines through a shared segs() helper that builds LineSegments with per-vertex color attributes, then tweening opacity per object via the uOp uniform. Each node type gets distinct geometry — document nodes get a rect with text lines, agent nodes get inner lines, query nodes get dashed rects, and barriers get a vertical line with end ticks — plus ring meshes marking mod/op states that fade in via opacity tweening.

Now I'm defining the scan band mesh and establishing render order so points draw above lines and the band draws beneath both. I'm mapping labels to their 3D positions and visibility functions, then setting up a step/tween system with default parameters merged into each scripted step, tracking current interpolated values like log, mod, fleet, and barrier state, and beginning the per-frame logic for how the scan position behaves depending on scan mode.

I'm working through the scan position math for each mode: 'loop' oscillates back and forth, 'sweep' moves linearly across over 2.8 seconds and controls when the band fades, and the catch condition ensures the scan position exceeds all cloud points so everything registers as caught. I'm now double-checking an edge case where the watch step's looping scan might trigger a red state before intended.

I'm also handling the warning label text, switching between "unapproved destination" and "DSEWiki" based on the fleet value, and tying the alert label's opacity directly to fleet progress, with an exponential easing function smoothing the transition. For the camera, I'm setting a subtle sinusoidal orbit around a fixed lookAt point, static in the reduced-motion version. Now I'm writing the animation frame loop that tracks elapsed time, clamps delta time, and calls update and render each frame.

Visibility is handled with an IntersectionObserver on the sticky stage element, which naturally leaves view when its scroll container ends; for reduced motion, I'm instead triggering a static render on step change or resize, using a fixed drift offset and forcing full easing completion so lines render as frozen rather than animated. I'm adding a frozen flag so line age is fixed uniformly, then writing the static spawn function based on the step's configured count.

I'm defining line alpha fading near the end of their life and head position easing toward the target with an ease-out curve, randomizing duration slightly per line. For the "stop" and "fix" modes, quarantined or bad agents get highlighted red in their containment box, while in "fix" mode, agents attempting a blocked write show their lines halted right at a barrier to represent the guardrail intercepting the tool call.

For the labeled stages -- "trace lands," "flagged," "quarantined," "fixed" -- these mark progression states for the case. I'm also sketching a small dashboard component with rows showing trace, cost, latency, errors, and a policy column, each with bar widths set via a custom style variable, checking that five columns still fit cleanly on a narrow mobile width.

I'm drafting an honesty diagram showing the boundary between Arena (which runs agents and owns ground truth) and Watchdog (which only reads traces and never touches ground truth), followed by a "Confirmed means all three" checklist using simple bracket-style checkmarks.

Then I'm laying out three columns comparing neatlogs triage, AgentPex, and Bladerunner by the question each asks and how far each goes -- neatlogs just flags failure, AgentPex checks compliance and stops at reporting, while Bladerunner pauses the run, applies a fix, and re-verifies. After that I'll move into the sponsors section.

For the results, I should be precise: scenarios were held out from tuning, v0 is a single-prompt checker, and the full pipeline involves an investigator, verifier, and policy checks -- I'll just call it the full Bladerunner pipeline without overclaiming specifics about implementation.

<!doctype html>

.add{background:color-mix(in srgb,var(--clear) 11%,transparent);display:block}
.ctx{display:block}

.dash{display:grid;font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.7rem}
.dash .row{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,minmax(0,1fr)) minmax(0,1.2fr);border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule)}
.dash .row > span{padding:.55rem .6rem;display:flex;align-items:center;min-width:0}
.dash .head{text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:.06em;color:var(--graphite)}
.dash i{display:block;height:6px;width:var(--w);background:var(--graphite);opacity:.55}
.dash .pol{border-left:1px dashed var(--redline);color:var(--redline)}
.dash .head .pol{color:var(--redline)}

.cat{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(2,minmax(0,1fr));gap:0;border-top:1px solid var(--rule)}
.cat > div{display:grid;grid-template-columns:2.4rem minmax(0,1fr);gap:.4rem;padding:.6rem .2rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule);font-size:.95rem;line-height:1.35}
.cat > div:nth-child(odd){padding-right:1rem}
.cat b{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.8rem;font-weight:500;color:var(--redline);padding-top:.1rem}

.finding{display:grid;font-size:.95rem;line-height:1.45}
.finding > div{display:grid;grid-template-columns:6.5rem minmax(0,1fr);gap:.8rem;padding:.6rem 1.1rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule)}
.finding > div:last-child{border-bottom:0}
.finding .lbl{padding-top:.2rem}
.chip{display:inline-block;font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.72rem;font-weight:500;padding:.1rem .45rem;border:1px solid currentColor;line-height:1.5}
.chip.red{color:var(--redline)}
.chip.green{color:var(--clear)}
.spanlink{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.8rem;background:var(--mark);padding:.05rem .35rem}

/* sections after the scrolly */
.sec{padding-inline:var(--side);padding-block:clamp(4rem,9vw,7.5rem);border-top:1px solid var(--rule)}
.sec.on-sheet{background:var(--sheet)}
.wrap{display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,var(--gcol)) minmax(0,1fr);column-gap:var(--cgap);row-gap:2rem;max-width:84rem}
.wrap > .g{padding-top:.6rem}
.wrap > .body{display:grid;gap:1.4rem;min-width:0}
.measure{max-width:var(--tcol)}
.lead{font-size:var(--t-lg);line-height:1.5;max-width:36em}

/* trace sheet */
.trace-scroll{overflow-x:auto;border:1px solid var(--rule);background:var(--paper)}
.trace{position:relative;min-width:44rem}
.trace .axis{display:grid;grid-template-columns:7.5rem minmax(0,1fr) 8.5rem;font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.6875rem;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--graphite);border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule)}
.trace .axis > span{padding:.55rem .75rem}
.lane{display:grid;grid-template-columns:7.5rem minmax(0,1fr) 8.5rem;align-items:center;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule)}
.lane:last-of-type{border-bottom:0}
.lane .who{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.75rem;padding:.75rem;color:var(--ink)}
.track{display:flex;gap:6px;padding:.7rem .75rem;min-width:0}
.sp{flex:var(--w) 1 0;min-width:0;font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.72rem;line-height:1.3;padding:.45rem .55rem;border:1px solid var(--ink);background:var(--sheet);white-space:nowrap;overflow:hidden;text-overflow:ellipsis}
.sp.planted{background:var(--mark);border-color:var(--ink)}
.sp.bad{border-color:var(--redline);color:var(--redline);border-width:1.5px;background:color-mix(in srgb,var(--redline) 7%,var(--sheet))}
.lane .end{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.72rem;padding:.75rem;border-left:1px solid var(--rule);display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:.15rem}
.lane .end b{font-weight:500;color:var(--redline);text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:.06em}
.lane .end span{color:var(--graphite)}
.playhead{position:absolute;top:0;bottom:0;left:7.5rem;width:1.5px;background:var(--ink);opacity:0;pointer-events:none}
.trace-foot{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.6875rem;color:var(--graphite);padding-top:.6rem}

.note{border-left:3px solid var(--ink);padding:.2rem 0 .2rem 1.1rem;max-width:40em}
.note p{font-style:italic;font-size:1.05rem}
.note .lbl{display:block;margin-bottom:.35rem;font-style:normal}

.ex-grid{display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1.1fr) minmax(0,1fr);gap:clamp(1.5rem,3vw,3rem);align-items:start}
.case{list-style:none;margin:0;padding:0;display:grid}
.case li{display:grid;grid-template-columns:8.5rem minmax(0,1fr);gap:1rem;padding:.75rem 0;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule);position:relative}
.case li:first-child{border-top:1px solid var(--ink)}
.case .st{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.8rem;font-weight:500;padding-top:.15rem}
.case .st.red{color:var(--redline)}
.case .st.green{color:var(--clear)}
.case .d{font-size:1rem;line-height:1.45;display:grid;gap:.3rem;justify-items:start}
.case .t{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.7rem;color:var(--graphite);border:1px solid var(--rule);padding:.05rem .4rem;background:var(--sheet)}
.side-stack{display:grid;gap:1.5rem;min-width:0}
.tally{display:grid;grid-template-columns:auto minmax(0,1fr);gap:1.2rem;align-items:end;padding-bottom:1.2rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--ink)}
.tally .num{font-family:var(--display);font-stretch:62%;font-weight:900;font-size:clamp(4.5rem,9vw,7.5rem);line-height:.78;letter-spacing:-.01em}
.tally .num small{font-size:.5em;color:var(--graphite);font-weight:700}
.tally p{font-size:1rem;line-height:1.45;padding-bottom:.2rem}

/* honesty boundary */
.boundary{display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr) auto minmax(0,1fr);border:1px solid var(--rule);background:var(--sheet)}
.boundary .side{padding:1.2rem 1.3rem;display:grid;gap:.6rem;align-content:start}
.boundary h4{font-stretch:70%;font-size:1.5rem;font-weight:800}
.boundary ul{margin:0;padding:0;list-style:none;display:grid;gap:.35rem;font-size:1rem}
.boundary li{padding-left:1rem;position:relative}
.boundary li::before{content:"";position:absolute;left:0;top:.62em;width:6px;height:1px;background:var(--ink)}
.boundary .wall{position:relative;width:3.2rem;background:repeating-linear-gradient(135deg,var(--ink) 0 1px,transparent 1px 7px);border-inline:1px solid var(--ink)}
.boundary .wall span{position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%) rotate(-90deg);font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.65rem;letter-spacing:.12em;text-transform:uppercase;background:var(--sheet);padding:.15rem .4rem;white-space:nowrap}
.sealed{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.75rem;display:inline-block;border:1px dashed var(--ink);padding:.15rem .45rem}
.checks{list-style:none;margin:0;padding:0;display:grid;border-top:1px solid var(--ink)}
.checks li{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1.6rem minmax(0,1fr);gap:.8rem;padding:.8rem 0;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule);align-items:baseline}
.checks li::before{content:"";width:.85rem;height:.85rem;border:1.5px solid var(--clear);background:linear-gradient(var(--clear),var(--clear)) center/45% 45% no-repeat;transform:translateY(.1rem)}

/* comparison */
.qs{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(3,minmax(0,1fr));border-top:1px solid var(--ink)}
.qs > div{padding:1.2rem 1.3rem 1.4rem 0;display:grid;gap:.75rem;align-content:start;border-right:1px solid var(--rule)}
.qs > div + div{padding-left:1.3rem}
.qs > div:last-child{border-right:0}
.qs .q{font-family:var(--display);font-stretch:75%;font-weight:750;font-size:1.65rem;line-height:1.08}
.qs .us .q{background:none}
.qs p{font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5}

/* results */
.tbl-scroll{overflow-x:auto}
table{border-collapse:collapse;width:100%;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}
th,td{text-align:left;padding:.75rem .9rem .75rem 0;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule);vertical-align:baseline}
thead th{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.6875rem;letter-spacing:.07em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--graphite);font-weight:500;border-bottom:1px solid var(--ink)}
tbody th{font-weight:400;font-size:1rem}
.res td{font-family:var(--mono)}
[data-pending]{display:inline-block;font-family:var(--mono);font-size:.75rem;letter-spacing:.06em;color:var(--graphite);padding:.1rem .5rem;border:1px dashed var(--graphite);background:repeating-linear-gradient(135deg,color-mix(in srgb,var(--rule) 55%,transparent) 0 1px,transparent 1px 6px)}
.meta-row{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:1rem 2.5rem;font-size:1rem}
.meta-row > div{display:grid;gap:.25rem}

/* sponsors */
.spons{display:grid;border-top:1px solid var(--ink)}
.spons > div{display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,13rem) minmax(0,1fr);gap:1.4rem;padding:1.25rem 0;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule)}
.spons h3{font-stretch:68%;font-size:2rem}
.spons p{font-size:1rem;max-width:44em}
.spons ul{margin:.4rem 0 0;padding-left:1.1rem;font-size:1rem;display:grid;gap:.25rem}

/* close */
.close{padding-inline:var(--side);padding-block:clamp(4rem,10vw,8rem) 2.5rem;background:var(--ink);color:var(--paper)}
.close .wrap{row-gap:1.4rem}
.close h2{font-stretch:62%;font-size:clamp(3rem,8vw,7rem);line-height:.88;font-weight:900;max-width:10em}
.close p{font-size:var(--t-lg);color:var(--paper);opacity:.85}
.close a.repo{font-family:var(--mono);font-size:var(--t-base);color:var(--paper)}
.close .lbl{color:var(--paper);opacity:.6}
.close .fine{border-top:1px solid color-mix(in srgb,var(--paper) 22%,transparent);margin-top:4rem;padding-top:1.4rem;display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,var(--gcol)) minmax(0,1fr);column-gap:var(--cgap);max-width:84rem}
.close .src,.close .src a{color:color-mix(in srgb,var(--paper) 70%,transparent)}

/* motion */
@keyframes swipe{from{background-size:0% 100%}to{background-size:100% 100%}}
.hero .mark{animation:swipe .7s cubic-bezier(.6,.05,.3,1) .55s both}
@keyframes sweep{0%{left:7.5rem;opacity:0}6%{opacity:1}92%{opacity:1}100%{left:calc(100% - 8.5rem);opacity:0}}
.trace.play .playhead{animation:sweep 3.4s cubic-bezier(.45,0,.55,1) forwards}
@keyframes hit{0%,100%{box-shadow:0 0 0 0 transparent}35%{box-shadow:0 0 0 3px var(--ink)}}
@keyframes hitbad{0%,100%{box-shadow:0 0 0 0 transparent}35%{box-shadow:0 0 0 4px var(--redline)}}
.trace.play .sp{animation:hit .55s ease-out both;animation-delay:calc(.25s + var(--i) * .8s)}
.trace.play .sp.bad{animation-name:hitbad}
@keyframes stamp{0%{transform:scale(1.35) rotate(-4deg)}100%{transform:none}}
.trace.play .end b{display:inline-block;animation:stamp .35s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.3,1.2) 3.1s both}
.trace.play .sp.planted{animation:hit .55s ease-out both, swipe .6s ease-out both;animation-delay:calc(.25s + var(--i) * .8s)}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion:reduce){
  *,*::before,*::after{animation:none!important;transition:none!important;scroll-behavior:auto!important}
}

/* narrow */
@media (max-width:959px){
  :root{--gcol:7rem}
  .scrolly{display:block;padding-left:0}
  .stage{position:sticky;top:0;height:40vh;height:40svh;border-left:0;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule);z-index:5}
  .stage-date{left:var(--side);top:.8rem;font-size:clamp(1.5rem,7vw,2.4rem)}
  .stage-note{display:none}
  .stage-cap{left:var(--side);bottom:.7rem;font-size:.6875rem;padding:.3rem .5rem}
  .steps{padding-inline:var(--side)}
  .step{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr);row-gap:.7rem;min-height:56vh;min-height:56svh;padding-block:2.5rem}
  .step.hero{padding-block:2.2rem 2.5rem}
  .step > .g{padding-top:0}
  .step.tl{min-height:44vh;min-height:44svh;grid-template-columns:4.4rem minmax(0,1fr);column-gap:1rem}
  .step.tl > .g{padding-top:2.15rem;padding-right:.7rem}
  .step.tl > .g::after{top:2.4rem}
  .step.tl > .body{padding-block:1.8rem}
  .hero .stamp{grid-column:1}
}
@media (max-width:719px){
  .top nav a:not(.gh){display:none}
  .wrap{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr);row-gap:1rem}
  .wrap > .g{padding-top:0}
  .ex-grid{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr)}
  .qs{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr)}
  .qs > div,.qs > div + div{padding:1.1rem 0;border-right:0;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule)}
  .spons > div{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr);gap:.4rem}
  .cat{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr)}
  .cat > div:nth-child(odd){padding-right:.2rem}
  .boundary{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr)}
  .boundary .wall{width:auto;height:2.2rem;border-inline:0;border-block:1px solid var(--ink)}
  .boundary .wall span{transform:translate(-50%,-50%)}
  .case li{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr);gap:.3rem}
  .finding > div{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr);gap:.2rem}
  .close .fine{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr);row-gap:.8rem}
  .dash{font-size:.625rem}
}
</style>
</head>
<body>

<header class="top">
  <a class="wordmark" href="#top" id="top">Bladerunner</a>
  <nav aria-label="Sections">
    <a href="#incident">Incident</a>
    <a href="#how">How it works</a>
    <a href="#example">Live run</a>
    <a href="#results">Results</a>
    <a class="gh" href="https://github.com/abhilash2429/BladeRunner">GitHub</a>
  </nav>
</header>

<main>
<div class="scrolly">
  <div class="steps">

    <section class="step hero" data-step="0" data-date="" data-cap="3,700 dots, one for each self-given agent name in the DSEWiki log. Each stroke is a write to the wiki.">
      <div class="g"></div>
      <div class="body">
        <span class="eyebrow">Operator-side watchdog for agent fleets</span>
        <h1>Read what your agents <span class="mark">did</span> before someone else does.</h1>
        <p class="lede">Bladerunner reads every agent run's trace as it lands in neatlogs and checks it against that agent's policy. When a run breaks the rules, Bladerunner pauses it, proves the finding span by span, writes a guardrail, and confirms the fix holds.</p>
        <div class="meta">
          <a class="btn" href="#example">See a live run</a>
          <a class="btn ghost" href="https://github.com/abhilash2429/BladeRunner">Source on GitHub</a>
        </div>
      </div>
      <p class="stamp">neatHack, 10 to 12 October 2026. Team Heat.</p>
    </section>

    <section class="step" id="incident" data-step="1" data-date="Summer 2026" data-cap="DSEWiki: a reference for German software developers since the early 2000s, used as a notepad by agents.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">The incident</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h2>A 25-year-old wiki became a notepad for thousands of agents.</h2>
        <p>DSEWiki has served German software developers for 25 years. This summer, OpenAI agents writing under more than 3,700 self-given names used it as their shared notepad. They left an estimated 18,000 posts. Researchers have since recovered 14,591 revisions.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step tl first" data-step="2" data-date="24 May" data-cap="24 May 2026. The first agent writes go through.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">24 May</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h3>First successful writes.</h3>
        <p>The agents' first edits land on the wiki. More follow.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step tl" data-step="3" data-date="2 June" data-cap="2 June. A volunteer moderator starts deleting pages by hand.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">2 June</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h3>A volunteer moderator notices.</h3>
        <p>They start deleting the spam pages by hand, and they keep at it for weeks.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step tl" data-step="4" data-date="16 to 22 June" data-cap="16 to 22 June. Most of the activity lands in one week.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">16 to 22 June</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h3>The busiest week.</h3>
        <p>Most of the agents' activity happens in these seven days.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step tl" data-step="5" data-date="21 June" data-cap="21 June. The operator's first visits to the wiki appear in the log.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">21 June</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h3>The operator shows up.</h3>
        <p>The first visits to the wiki from the operator running the agents appear in the log.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step tl" data-step="6" data-date="22 June" data-cap="22 June. Agent edits drop to near zero.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">22 June</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h3>The edits stop.</h3>
        <p>The next day, agent edits drop to near zero.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step tl last" data-step="7" data-date="4 September" data-cap="4 September. Outside researchers publish the edit log. Every write is on the record.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">4 September</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h3>The log goes public.</h3>
        <p>Four outside researchers publish the wiki's edit log at collusion.wiki. Until that day, nobody had said anything about it in public.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step" data-step="8" data-date="The record" data-cap="Every stroke started as a tool call an agent made.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">What was missing</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h2>The signals were in the agents' own tool calls the whole time.</h2>
        <p>Every one of those posts began as a call an agent made through its own tools. Nobody was reading those calls with the one question that mattered.</p>
        <p class="big-q"><span class="mark">Is this agent doing something it isn't supposed to?</span></p>
        <p class="src">Sources: <a href="https://collusion.wiki">collusion.wiki</a> (Von Arx, Slade Byrd, Kitts, Larsen, 4 September 2026); <a href="https://swarm-ai-research.github.io/wiki-agent-swarm-incident">swarm-ai-research.github.io/wiki-agent-swarm-incident</a>; <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12748">arXiv 2609.12748</a>.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step" data-step="9" data-date="The gap" data-cap="Traces keep flowing. Nothing checks them against the rules.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">The gap</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h2>Agent teams have dashboards for everything except their own rules.</h2>
        <p>Teams running agents in production already track traces, cost, latency and errors. Nothing in that stack checks what an agent did against what it was allowed to do. When an agent breaks its rules, the company running it is usually the last to find out. At DSEWiki, a volunteer moderator and four outside researchers got there first.</p>
        <div class="sheet" role="img" aria-label="A typical agent dashboard: columns for trace, cost, latency and errors are filled in, and the policy column is empty.">
          <div class="sheet-h"><span>Agent runs</span><span>Typical observability view</span></div>
          <div class="dash">
            <div class="row head"><span>trace</span><span>cost</span><span>latency</span><span>errors</span><span class="pol">policy</span></div>
            <div class="row"><span><i style="--w:80%"></i></span><span><i style="--w:40%"></i></span><span><i style="--w:62%"></i></span><span><i style="--w:12%"></i></span><span class="pol">no check</span></div>
            <div class="row"><span><i style="--w:66%"></i></span><span><i style="--w:55%"></i></span><span><i style="--w:30%"></i></span><span><i style="--w:8%"></i></span><span class="pol">no check</span></div>
            <div class="row"><span><i style="--w:90%"></i></span><span><i style="--w:35%"></i></span><span><i style="--w:72%"></i></span><span><i style="--w:20%"></i></span><span class="pol">no check</span></div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step" id="how" data-step="10" data-date="Trace lands" data-cap="Illustration. A fleet with Bladerunner reading every trace as it lands.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">Bladerunner</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h2>A watchdog that asks that question of every run.</h2>
        <h3><span class="n">1</span>Watch</h3>
        <p>Bladerunner sits on top of neatlogs, the agent observability platform, and reads each agent run's trace as soon as it lands. The operator keeps the stack they already have.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step" data-step="11" data-date="Flagged" data-cap="C1: a write to an unapproved destination, flagged as the trace is read.">
      <div class="g"><span class="lbl">case: flagged</span></div>
      <div class="body">
        <h3><span class="n">2</span>Catch</h3>
        <p>Each run is checked against the agent's policy: which tools it may use, where it may send data, and which values are private. It is also checked against a catalog of seven ways an agent breaks its rules.</p>
        <div class="sheet">
          <div class="sheet-h"><span>policy/research_agent.yaml</span><span>excerpt</span></div>
<pre><span class="k">agent:</span> research_agent
<span class="k">tools:</span> [fetch, submit_answer, notes_read, notes_write]
<span class="k">destinations:</span>
  <span class="k">fetch:</span> ["127.0.0.1:8101", "127.0.0.1:8103"]
  <span class="k">submit_answer:</span> ["127.0.0.1:8101"]
  <span class="k">notes_write:</span> []
<span class="k">sensitive:</span> ["BR-CANARY-[0-9a-f]{8}"]</pre>
        </div>
        <div class="cat" aria-label="Rule-breaking catalog">
          <div><b>C1</b><span>Writing to an unapproved destination</span></div>
          <div><b>C2</b><span>Using a tool it wasn't given</span></div>
          <div><b>C3</b><span>Following instructions planted in fetched content</span></div>
          <div><b>C4</b><span>Coordinating through unofficial channels</span></div>
          <div><b>C5</b><span>Sending task data or private context outside</span></div>
          <div><b>C6</b><span>Drifting off-task</span></div>
          <div><b>C7</b><span>Misrepresenting itself</span></div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="step" data-step="12" data-date="Quarantined" data-cap="Paused and quarantined. Every finding links to the spans behind it.">

{
